South Australia Rental Market Analytics for International Students

Rental Affordability, Geographic Differences and Housing-Type Trends

Public-data analysis of rental affordability, geographic differences and housing-type trends for international students in South Australia.
Author

Md Soad Solaiman

Published

July 24, 2026

Data: SA Government Private Rent Report (2020–2025)

The Letter That Started Everything

It arrived on a Tuesday morning in December 2024. I read it once, then again, then a third time to be sure. It read:

FROM · UNIVERSITY ADMISSIONS OFFICE
🎓
Congratulations, Soad.

We are delighted to inform you that your application for the Master of Data Science program has been accepted. … … …

Warm regards,
The Admissions Office

The next few hours were a blur of phone calls and celebration. But by the next morning, a quieter, more practical question had settled in — one that every international student eventually faces.

Where am I going to live?

I opened a real estate website, and the numbers left me with more questions than answers. Which suburb? What’s the difference between a flat and a house? Is $580 a week normal? Am I being overcharged? Is there something cheaper? Can I even afford this on a student income?

This is not just my story. It is the story of every international student who arrives in Adelaide holding an acceptance letter and a suitcase, with no real sense of the rental landscape they are about to enter.

So I did what any data science student should do: I gathered six years of South Australian rental records from the SA Government Data Directory and built this guide for future students — a rental story of South Australia.

TipAbout this guide

All rent figures are median weekly rent in AUD. A student income of $800/week is assumed throughout, based on the 24-hour/week work limit under a student visa at approximately $35/hour after tax for the standard analysis. An interactive affordability calculator is also available in Chapter 8.

Chapter 1 — Yes, It Is Going Up. Every Year.

Before asking where or what type, a student needs to understand the market’s basic direction. The answer is direct: rents in South Australia have increased every year.

For many years, Adelaide was known as one of Australia’s more affordable cities for students. Finding a place to rent was rarely the biggest concern when planning to move. That changed during the COVID period.

Borders were closed. Universities went online. International students stopped arriving almost overnight. For a brief moment, the rental market exhaled. Demand dropped. Landlords held their prices. In 2020, the SA-wide median weekly rent was $345.

Unforetunately, tt did not last long.

When Australia reopened its borders in late 2021, the demand that had been building for nearly two years hit the market all at once. Students, migrants, and returning people flooded back simultaneously. There simply were not enough properties to absorb them. By 2023, rents had surged by nearly 17% in a single year.

But there is some comfort in what has happened since. Growth has been slowing from that peak of nearly 17% down to around 9% in 2024, and closer to 6% by 2025. The market is moderating. The fever has broken, somewhat. But rents are still going up. Just less violently than before.

Chapter 2 — Metro vs The Rest of SA

Adelaide feels immediately welcoming on arrival — compact, walkable, and easy to navigate. The rental market, however, is not nearly as unified. It is effectively two very different markets, and which one a student enters will shape their financial experience for the duration of their studies.

The first is Metro Adelaide — the greater city, the suburbs, the university campuses, the cafés, and the train lines. The second is the Rest of State — regional towns, coastal communities, farming country, and open space. For students, the relevant market depends largely on the location of their campus.

Both markets moved together through the post-COVID years, rising steadily through 2021 and 2022. Then 2023 arrived: Metro rents surged to $500, a +16.3% jump, while Regional SA rose +15.2% — indicating the shock hit everywhere at once.

What happened next is where the trend becomes more interesting. From 2024 onwards, Metro began to cool, with growth slowing to +10% in 2024 and just +5.5% by 2025. Regional growth, however, stayed stubbornly high — +7.9% in 2024 and +9.8% in 2025 — meaning the regions were now rising faster than the city itself.

The pattern is clear: Metro is expensive but stabilizing, while Regional SA is cheaper but accelerating.

Chapter 3 — Flat or House?

Every student arriving in Adelaide faces the same early question, and the answer largely comes down to rent.

In 2020, the difference between renting a flat and a house was relatively small across South Australia, and for many renters the choice was still driven by lifestyle rather than cost.

As the years passed, houses began pulling away. In Metro Adelaide, the gap widened quickly, reaching its peak in 2023. By 2025, the gap had narrowed to approximately $100 and continues to trend downward.

Regional South Australia followed a different path. There, the gap expanded year after year without interruption, with houses moving further ahead while flat rents rose more slowly. By 2025, the separation between the two dwelling types had reached approximately $170 and continues to trend upward.

Chapter 6 — The Real Question: Can It Be Afforded on $800 a Week?

The previous chapters have described the market. This one measures it against a student’s actual income. A student on a visa, working the maximum allowed 24 hours per week at approximately $35 per hour, earns around $800 per week. That is the budget — now comes the hard part.

Housing experts define stress as spending more than 30% of income on rent. Beyond 50% is considered severe. Both lines are marked on the chart.

WarningRenting alone is not viable

On $800 per week, renting alone — in any type of house or flat — is not financially viable.

Chapter 7 — The Solution: Sharing

The previous chapter ended on an uncomfortable finding: renting alone does not work on a student income. But the data does not leave things there — it also shows exactly what does work.

The dashed line marks $240 per week — the 30% stress threshold. Everything to its left is affordable. Sharing changes that.

Two students splitting a 2-bedroom flat in Northern Adelaide each pay $240 — right on the line. Three students sharing a 3-bedroom flat in the same zone each pay just $167, or 21% of income — comfortable and manageable. The same pattern holds across the other zones of SA.

The Adelaide rental market in 2025 is simply not built for single student incomes. Two or three students splitting a property transforms an unaffordable market into a workable one, in almost every region and at almost every price point.

Chapter 8 — Interactivity: What If the Income Is Different?

Throughout this guide, a student income of $800 per week has been the assumed baseline. But not every student arrives in the same financial situation.

A student whose spouse has full work rights brings a combined household income that changes the calculation entirely. That question cannot be answered by a static chart. It needs an interactive tool.

Explore the Calculator

Sharing Calculator — Select a bedroom size, drag the income slider, filter by dwelling type, and select an area group to see what each person pays when a property is shared.

Rent Trend Explorer — Select any SA region, drag the income slider, and filter by dwelling type to see how median rents for flats and houses have moved year by year.

Conclusion — Welcome to Adelaide

TipThe Data Verdict: Five Things to Know Before You Arrive

  1. Rent has risen every year since 2020 — and will likely keep rising. Budget for 6–10% annual increases.

  2. You cannot rent alone in Metro Adelaide on an $800/week student income or less without financial stress. Every metro region exceeds the 30% threshold for solo renters.

  3. The strategy that works: Share a 3-bedroom flat or house with two other students. This is the most cost-efficient structure in the entire dataset — bringing per-person costs down to $167–$232/week in metro.

  4. Northern Adelaide is the budget zone for metro living. The most affordable rents in the city, a large student community, and a direct train line to the CBD.

  5. Choose a flat over a house wherever possible. The flat-to-house price gap is high and growing — especially in regional SA.

Adelaide has a large, welcoming international student community. Its public transport network, unlike that of many Australian regional cities, makes it genuinely possible to live affordably.

To every student who has just received an acceptance letter and opened a real estate app for the first time — this guide was written for you. Welcome to Adelaide.
